Thank you for submitting your article "Thermosensitive alternative splicing senses and mediates temperature adaptation in Drosophila" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Mani Ramaswami as Reviewing Editor and Ronald Calabrese as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

The reviewers note that work linking generation of a 18C-specific, timeless splice isoform Tim-Sc to temperature-adaption of the circadian clock has been improved and tightened by several additional experiments. New analysis of Tim-Sc Per interactions and as well as phenotypic effects of tim-sc expression in per0 flies are consistent with that Tim-sc triggered, PER independent (but yet unspecified) mechanisms in temperature-adaptation of circadian clock.

However, the manuscript requires extensive text revisions and some simple experimental additions before it can be considered acceptable for publication. The text is dense, difficult to read and appears to have been hastily assembled and needs a fair bit of work to make it more reader-friendly. It also contains several errors including an incorrect description of tim-sc which is fundamental to this manuscript and missing references. Further, it includes statements that are not supported by the data. Several very general claims about the tim splicing representing general cellular thermometers go way beyond the results – when a simple experiments exist to determine whether this may be true or not. Several, lines of changes are required. First, the manuscript needs to be carefully edited for clarity, grammar and accuracy to be easily accessible and comprehensive to the reader. And second, particularly given that the conclusions, while interesting are not decisive with respect to the mechanism by which Tim-Sc works, some key behavioral experiments (comments 12, 13) should also be conducted at colder temperatures (18 °C) to better test implications that the RNA modelling suggests for stability changes with temperature.

Major comments:

1) The opening sentence makes no sense – ' degradation of genes'? Maybe 'clock gene products'?

2) 'little is known…’ appears to be a bit harsh? Others who work in the field such as Ralf Stanewsky and Isaac Edery may disagree with this and perhaps their insights should be acknowledged.

3) Introduction, third paragraph. TIM is not the key factor, it's a key factor.

4) Introduction, third paragraph. tim is the key factor for light signalling' not 'TIM is the key pathway for conveying external information to the circadian system at the molecular level.' The authors are overplaying the role of TIM in all environmental inputs, light, temperature, social, etc. This is incorrect…

5) Introduction, fourth paragraph. Majercak et al., 2004, should also be cited along with Collins et al., 2004.

6) Introduction, fourth paragraph. The Edery group has done a lot of additional work on per splicing which has clarified somewhat how per splicing might impinge on thermal adaptation. Should be elaborated a little here.

7) Most figures – the authors need to state what the error bars represent -SEMS?

8) Subsection “Temperature modulates tim alternative splicing”, first paragraph – there is a 3 fold increase at low temperature of per spliced, so tim is not the only clock gene with a significant thermal splicing pattern. Also Montelli et al., 2015, showed that at 10 °C per spliced reflects about 50% of total transcript and tim-cold about 90% of tim transcript at this temperature even though overall tim levels are low. It is surprising that this highly relevant study is not even mentioned or cited. We note that it is mentioned in the third paragraph of the Discussion in a different context but does not appear in the references.

9) 'In contrast to the other isoforms which are generated by intron retention, tim-sc mRNA is generated by the usage of an alternative cleavage and polyadenylation site located within the intron 10 of tim which can only be used before this intron is spliced out.'

10) Apart from being ungrammatical, this sentence makes no biological sense. The authors suggest that the intron is spliced out. If so how can the STOP, cleavage and polyA sites be used? Surely this intron or part of it must also be retained?

11) 'As mentioned above, this isoform appears only at 18 °C, strongly suggesting that this isoform is responsible for the adaptation to cold temperatures'. This is an intuitive leap based on a correlation – no causation can be implied at this stage. If this was the case would not one expect higher levels of tim-sc and tim-cold in D. virilis at colder temperatures? So why is it 'surprising' that D. virilis does show higher levels of tim-cold at lower temperatures Doesn't the presence of tim-cold in all species at higher levels at colder temperatures argue that this is the conserved, important transcript for cold adaptation?

12) Figure 5 – Why was the behavioral analysis nor also performed at 18 °C given that all this is done in a WT background? This needs to be done and included and the findings discussed.

13) Figure 6A to C. Again, might it not be useful to examine rescue of tim01 at lower temperature? Perhaps the different UTRs are more or less stable at different temperatures? This appears to be worth a shot perhaps given the last section on RNA structure?

14) 'These results demonstrate that despite the smaller size, tim-sc encodes a fully functional TIM protein'. Why 'fully' with only 42% rescue?

15) 'Control flies presented two different responses when transferred to 18 °C: a delay of the evening component as well as a decreased night activity in comparison to the flies maintained at 25 °C '(Figure 6C, 6D and 6E).' Do the authors mean Figure 7C, D, E.

16) 'In addition, the activity patterns of 40A flies are strikingly similar at the different temperatures.' Not really, and no more similar than controls. If one examines panels 7D and 7E the two phenotypes change more in 40A than in controls.

17) 'Last but not least, our data suggest that tim alternative splicing might act as a thermometer for the cell.' This is a very general statement, not even limited to the circadian clock. If this is the case then other temperature dependent phenotypes should also be affected by the tim-splicing mutants. Why don't the authors check one of these out, for example the temperature at which temperature-sensitive mutants become paralysed e.g. shits, parats etc? Simple enough to do but unlikely to support the authors general claim.

results.result: Temperature remodels the circadian transcriptome with most cycling RNAs being temperature-specific. Hundreds of genes show oscillating expression at 18°C, 25°C, or 29°C, but only a few oscillate at all temperatures. Different Gene Ontology terms are enriched at each temperature, demonstrating temperature-dependent circadian programming.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by 3' RNA-seq data (Figure 1A-B) and GO analysis (Supplementary file 2). The data clearly show temperature-specific cycling patterns and different functional enrichments at different temperatures, providing strong evidence for temperature-dependent circadian transcriptional programs.

results.result: Core circadian clock genes show a phase advance at 18°C relative to 25°C or 29°C. The phase advance in tim and per mRNA is transcriptional and results in advanced TIM and PER protein levels, mirroring the behavioral advance of evening activity at lower temperatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1C), chromatin-bound RNA analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and previous research. The transcriptional nature of the phase advance is demonstrated, and the connection to protein levels and behavior is established through current and cited data.

results.result: Temperature dramatically changes tim alternative splicing patterns. Four major isoforms (tim-L, tim-cold, tim-sc, tim-M) are identified with distinct temperature-dependent expression. At 18°C, tim-cold and tim-sc are abundant; at 29°C, tim-M is elevated while tim-sc and tim-cold are absent. These changes are more dramatic than those observed for per splicing.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C99 are comprehensively supported by whole-transcript RNA-seq (Figure 2A-D), 3' RNA-seq (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and qRT-PCR validation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). The characterization of four isoforms with distinct temperature-dependent patterns is well-documented with multiple complementary approaches.

results.result: Temperature-dependent tim splicing changes observed in whole heads are also present in dissected brains. At 18°C, tim-sc and tim-cold levels increase in the brain, while at 29°C, tim-M expression is promoted.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 are supported by qRT-PCR data from dissected brains (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), demonstrating that the temperature-dependent splicing changes are not artifacts of whole-head analysis but occur in the relevant circadian tissue.

results.result: Temperature-dependent tim splicing is conserved across Drosophila species and correlates with behavioral temperature adaptation. D. melanogaster and D. simulans show similar behavioral adaptation and tim splicing patterns, including tim-sc expression only at 18°C. D. yakuba shows reduced temperature adaptation and lacks tim-sc. D. virilis shows unusual tim-cold expression at all temperatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C123 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 3A) and RNA-seq analysis across species (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The correlation between behavioral adaptation capacity and tim splicing patterns across species provides strong comparative evidence for the functional importance of tim splicing in temperature adaptation.

results.result: TIM-L protein levels are reduced at 18°C despite unchanged total tim mRNA levels. tim-M mRNA is abundant but the protein is not detected, suggesting it is not translated or translated inefficiently. The lower TIM-L levels at 18°C result from post-transcriptional/post-translational regulation and deviation of transcription toward tim-sc and tim-cold.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C131 are supported by western blot data, RNA-seq data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and citations to previous work. The absence of TIM-M protein despite high mRNA levels is clearly demonstrated, and the inference about post-transcriptional regulation is well-supported by the data showing unchanged total mRNA but decreased protein.

results.result: tim isoforms are differentially regulated by miRNAs in a temperature-dependent manner. AGO1 binding to tim-L/M/cold is strong at 18°C but weak at 25°C/29°C. tim-sc is not regulated by miRNAs. Luciferase assays show tim-cold 3'UTR strongly reduces expression. miR-969 is upregulated at 18°C. miRNA-mediated control imposes thresholds that limit expression of tim-cold and tim-M at non-permissive temperatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C152 are supported by AGO1 immunoprecipitation (Figure 4A-B), luciferase reporter assays (Figure 4C), TargetScan analysis (Figure 4D), and small RNA sequencing (Figure 4E-F). The multi-layered evidence from different experimental approaches provides strong support for temperature-dependent miRNA regulation of specific tim isoforms.

results.result: Overexpression of different TIM isoforms has distinct effects on circadian behavior. TIM-SC overexpression advances evening activity and shortens period. TIM-L overexpression causes long/weak rhythms. TIM-COLD has intermediate effects. TIM-M overexpression has no significant effect, suggesting it is non-functional.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C163 are supported by behavioral data from overexpression experiments (Figure 5A-D). The distinct behavioral phenotypes for each isoform provide functional evidence for their different roles, with TIM-SC showing the most distinctive phenotype of period shortening and phase advance.

results.result: TIM-SC rescues tim01 mutant behavioral rhythms in both LD and DD conditions. In LD, >60% of flies show evening anticipation rescue; in DD, >40% show rhythmic behavior with shorter periods than TIM-L rescue. This demonstrates TIM-SC is functional despite its smaller size.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C170 are supported by behavioral rescue experiments (Figure 6A-C). The partial rescue by TIM-SC in both LD and DD conditions, with characteristic short periods, provides strong functional evidence that this truncated protein can support circadian rhythms, though the rescue is incomplete (possibly due to overexpression levels as noted in C165).

results.result: TIM-SC binds to PER but does not stabilize it, unlike TIM-L which strongly stabilizes PER. TIM-SC can bind PER even in the presence of TIM-L. A small fraction (~19%) of per01 flies overexpressing TIM-SC show evening activity in LD but not in DD, suggesting TIM-SC can function partially independently of PER in some conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C180 are supported by co-transfection experiments in S2 cells (Figure 6D-E) and behavioral experiments in per01 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). The biochemical data clearly show differential effects on PER stabilization, and the partial rescue of per01 flies provides evidence for some PER-independent function, though this is limited and context-dependent.

results.result: CRISPR-generated tim-sc null mutants (40A) show altered locomotor activity patterns at multiple temperatures. At 25°C, 40A flies display cold-like activity patterns with delayed evening activity onset. Total tim mRNA is unchanged, but tim-cold and tim-L/M levels are increased. The mutants show some temperature adaptation, possibly mediated by increased tim-cold.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C193 are supported by qRT-PCR validation of the mutation (Figure 7B), behavioral analysis (Figure 7C-E), and isoform-specific qRT-PCR (Figure 7F). The behavioral phenotypes are clear and consistent, and the molecular changes in other isoforms provide mechanistic insight. However, the hypothesis about tim-cold mediating residual adaptation (C193) is speculative and would benefit from additional validation.

results.result: Temperature-dependent tim splicing is independent of the circadian clock. Similar splicing patterns (higher tim-cold/tim-sc and lower tim-M at 18°C vs 29°C) are observed in wild-type, tim01, and per01 flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C194-C195 are supported by qRT-PCR data from clock mutants (Figure 8A) and consistent with previous findings for per splicing. The similar temperature-dependent splicing patterns in clock mutants demonstrate that the splicing response is not dependent on a functional circadian clock.

results.result: Splice site strength analysis reveals that constitutive tim introns have strong 5' and 3' splice sites, while temperature-sensitive introns (tim-M, tim-cold) have strong 5' but weak 3' splice sites. The tim-sc intron has strong sites at both ends. This pattern is conserved in D. simulans and D. yakuba.
results.evaluation: Claims C196-C199 are supported by computational splice site strength analysis (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The correlation between splice site strength and temperature sensitivity provides mechanistic insight, though the analysis is computational and would benefit from experimental validation of the predicted effects.

results.result: Temperature-dependent tim splicing is reproduced in S2 cells expressing CLK and in minigene experiments. The same temperature-dependent patterns are observed in vitro as in vivo, with no temperature effect on constitutive exons, demonstrating a direct and specific effect of temperature on tim alternative splicing.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C204 are supported by qRT-PCR from S2 cells (Figure 8B) and minigene experiments (Figure 8D). The reproduction of temperature-dependent splicing in simplified systems (S2 cells and minigenes) provides strong evidence that the temperature sensing is intrinsic to the tim sequences themselves, not requiring complex cellular context.

results.result: RNA secondary structure predictions suggest a mechanism for temperature-sensitive splicing. The 5' splice sites of cold-retained introns (tim-sc, tim-cold) are predicted to form strong secondary structures that would be more stable at lower temperatures, reducing accessibility. The tim-M intron 5' splice site lacks strong secondary structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C205-C208 are based on computational RNA structure predictions (Figure 8—figure supplement 2) and theoretical reasoning about RNA stability at different temperatures. While the predictions are consistent with the observed splicing patterns, these are computational predictions without experimental validation. The hypothesis is plausible but requires experimental testing (e.g., mutagenesis of predicted structures, direct measurement of structure at different temperatures) to be considered supported.

results.result: Temperature dramatically changes tim splicing in Drosophila, inducing cold-specific isoforms (tim-cold, tim-sc) at 18°C and tim-M at 29°C. tim-sc encodes a functional protein that rescues tim01 mutants. Flies lacking tim-sc have abnormal locomotor activity. miRNA-mediated control limits expression of some isoforms. tim alternative splicing may act as a thermometer for the circadian clock.
results.evaluation: This is the main result summarizing the key findings. Claims C2-C8 are supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence throughout the manuscript, including RNA-seq, behavioral assays, rescue experiments, CRISPR mutants, and miRNA analysis. The thermometer hypothesis (C8) is supported by minigene data showing intrinsic temperature sensitivity, though the mechanism requires further investigation.
